channel.title: bfo.mantis: new releases
channel.description: New songs and instrumentals from bfo.mantis (bfo.mantis Records).

item.title: Cake on the Plate (single)
item.description: Cake on the Plate is a dark martial anthem about how Sparta really fell. The three hundred hold the Hot Gates with oil on their skin and shields locked in the pass, then the gold rolls home in Persian carts. Boys who slept on stone sleep on down, spears hang as ornaments, and the iron goes soft at the table, not at the gates.

item.title: For Your Own Good (single)
item.description: For Your Own Good is dark protest rock that sings its warning like a lullaby. From Juvenal's bread and games to parish care, wartime papers and emergencies that never end, every chain arrives wearing a favor and asking only for the keys. Hard times forge the builders; soft times hand the keys away. The velvet comes off the blade, and one lone voice answers with a single word: No.

item.title: Freeborn (single)
item.description: Freeborn is a roll-call rock anthem about the one right nobody hands you. It marches from a London pillory to an emperor's table at Worms, a Maryland farm, a Montgomery bus and a Prague square, and finds the same thing at every stop: a crown built on a million nods, brought down by a single No.

item.title: Unextracted (single)
item.description: Unextracted is a taut rock anthem about the one thing no contract can take. The papers slide across the table, they price the breath and offer silver for the hand, but the pulse under the wrist keeps its own time. The song insists that pulse was never theirs to claim.

item.title: Crown of Ash (single)
item.description: Crown of Ash is a slow, solemn reckoning sung to a fallen tyrant in the style of an old ballad. The narrator weighs mercy against the widows, orphans and graves the ruler left behind, and the song ends in a stillness that feels less like victory than a long-held breath finally let go.

item.title: The Only Way (single)
item.description: A cold-eyed sermon against polite compliance, arguing that ballots, petitions and good manners have never loosened a yoke. Its answer is refusal itself, held up as the one defense of liberty that has always worked.

item.title: Forge of Your Light (single)
item.description: A tribute to a mother pictured as a blacksmith who hammered seven children into shape in the forge of home. Faith, endurance and family legacy ring through every image of fire and tempered metal.

item.title: DANGEROUS (album)
item.description: DANGEROUS is built on one idea: a peaceful person who refuses to obey is far more powerful than a harmless one. Across 15 rock tracks, bfo.mantis takes aim at qualified immunity, unconstitutional laws, the language of official help and the people who enforce it, with history lessons from Marbury v. Madison to the 1946 Battle of Athens woven between the anger. The mood runs from stately hymns of vigilance to the most profane outbursts in the catalog, and every song comes back to the same choice between kneeling and standing.

item.title: Savage Serenade Volume 3 (album)
item.description: Savage Serenade Volume 3 keeps the series' habit of pairing calm with violence, but its calm words carry more weight: beside the gentle and quiet ones come somber, solemn, stoic and yearning, as in Somber Tempest, Solemn Edge and Stoic Rage. A few titles reverse the order, such as Savage Calm and Feral Lullaby, while Silk and Steel names a soft material and a hard one side by side, echoing the album's move from nylon strings to steel. The guitar starts out restrained, with sparse single notes and harmonics in a warm, close room, then passes through a mournful folk stretch and a fast, forceful peak before stacked guitars ring together like voices under a high vaulted roof. From there the sound thins to a last chiming harmonic and gives way to quiet, with Feral Lullaby as the closing word.

item.title: Road to Hell (single)
item.description: A blunt broadside against trading freedom for promised safety, built on the idea that kind language and good intentions disguise control. It takes hard positions on gun rights and abortion and keeps insisting that words carry real meaning.

item.title: Blood Waters the Tree (single)
item.description: A story-song about Elias Hart, a small-town blacksmith of quiet faith who takes up his hammer when tyrants seize his village. His last stand, and his parting words to his daughter beneath an old oak, turn sacrifice into an inheritance.

item.title: Sovereign Heart of Fire (album)
item.description: Sovereign Heart of Fire carries the catalog's language of liberty into worship. Its 15 Christian/Gospel songs move between prayers for the courage to defend God-given rights and quieter songs of surrender, grace and resilience, including the tender portrait Havilah. Fire runs through it as both judgment and renewal, and it closes with the singer handing the throne of his own heart to Christ.

item.title: Savage Serenade Volume 2 (album)
item.description: Savage Serenade Volume 2 is built on a single move: a quiet word placed in front of a violent one. Storms, fires and wild creatures are all softened in name, from Silent Tempest and Velvet Thunder to Soft Inferno and Quiet Claw, until Howling Calm and Tempests Lullaby turn the pattern around. The guitar traces a similar arc, starting with whispered single notes and glassy harmonics in what feels like a candlelit wooden room, then widening into a melancholy folk lament and a fast, thunderous climax before overdubbed guitars rise into a cathedral of sound. In the end it all thins out to one fading harmonic and silence, and the last title, Mellow Thunder, leaves the storm rumbling somewhere far off.

item.title: The Ridge (album)
item.description: The Ridge is a two-track Hip Hop/Rap release about the 1992 siege at Ruby Ridge, Idaho. The first track is a long, graphic spoken account told from the Weaver family's side, and the second turns the same story into a hook-driven rap. Both end as memorials to Sammy and Vicki Weaver.

item.title: Savage Serenade (album)
item.description: Savage Serenade asks one acoustic guitar to be two things at once. The titles spell it out, from Savage Surrender and Tender Carnage to Roses on the Blade and Edge of Softness, setting violence beside devotion in almost every name. The playing follows the same split: drifting harmonics and quiet classical lines break into blazing flamenco strumming and percussive tapping on the guitar body, then settle into a layered tremolo that slowly fades. It closes on Last Savage Prayer and Fiercely Grateful, where the fury and the tenderness finally sound like the same heart.

item.title: One Man INVICTUS (album)
item.description: One Man INVICTUS is a gallery of individuals who changed events by refusing to bend, including the Tank Man of Tiananmen Square, Thich Quang Duc, Desmond Doss, Francis Marion, Gandhi, Joan of Arc and Leonidas. Nearly every one of its 15 rock tracks is titled One Man, and together they argue that history turns on single acts of conscience, peaceful or not. It ends in prayer, widening one person's stand into a nation of them.

item.title: One Man - 站着 (single)
item.description: Sung in Mandarin, this retelling of the lone man who faced the tanks after the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre frames his stand as a God-given act of free will. It sets the horrors of the Mao era against one unarmed figure whose refusal still echoes.

item.title: Spellbound Volume 3 (album)
item.description: Spellbound Volume 3 tells a story of leaving and coming home, mostly in single words. It drifts off course with Wayward and Adrift, turns inward through Reflections, Resonance, Trance and Within, reaches Reunion and Bliss at its center, then cuts loose again with Untethered before Return brings it back and Last light and Flickering Glimpse let the light go out. The sound moves away from the first two volumes into slow, late-night lounge: a quiet heartbeat pulse, a deep double bass with warm walking lines and soft bowed notes, and wordless melodies that rise and fall like tides. It stays spacious and unhurried, with long silences between notes and a candlelit calm that settles over the record as it goes.

item.title: Rebel Anthem (album)
item.description: Rebel Anthem is bfo.mantis at its most militant, 15 metal tracks aimed at a machine of corrupt officials, courts, central banks and surveillance. Several songs return in reworked versions, and history threads through the whole record, from the Declaration of Independence to Andrew Jackson's bank war. It swings from plain-spoken definitions of tyranny and rebellion to the most apocalyptic imagery in the catalog.

item.title: The Savage Ledger (single)
item.description: A rapid-fire indictment that reads like a list of grievances: Patriot Act surveillance, the income tax, the Federal Reserve, civil asset forfeiture, qualified immunity and the national debt. It closes on a call to educate and awaken rather than despair.

item.title: Spellbound Volume 2 (album)
item.description: Spellbound Volume 2 trades the first volume's language of enchantment for the passing of time. Its titles watch a day burn down, from Morning Dew and Sun Down to Nightfall and Midnight Rain, while Sand of Time, Stolen Time and Endless Moments count what is slipping away and Firelight Embers and Embers follow a fire as it dies, all of it set in motion by an opening track called Fading. The sound moves between two worlds: slow, hazy late-night lo-fi built on distant piano, warm synth pads, vinyl crackle and a single ringing twangy note like a last ember, and fingerpicked acoustic country ballads with rolling thunder and soft rain behind them. Later tracks add light electric blues licks and muted ambient synths, so the storm and the fireside end up sharing the same long night.

item.title: Spellbound Volume 1 (album)
item.description: Spellbound Volume 1 is an album about being held, and its titles say so from first to last: it opens on Captive and closes on Taken, with Transfixed, Smitten, Spellbound and Mesmerized in between. Running against that pull are titles about motion and open air, such as Rhythms of the Heart, Groove, Traveling and Country Stars, along with a lone Stoic that sounds like someone trying not to fall. The music starts as an acoustic country rock ballad, with fingerpicked guitar, pedal steel and harmonica under rolling thunder and soft rain, then drifts into long, hazy late-night pieces built on lonely minor-key piano, shimmering guitars, warm synth pads and cello. Along the way it takes darker and more rhythmic turns, from harmonica over chill electronic beats to heavy metal guitars slowed and softened into lo-fi calm, before faint wind and rain return at the close, as if the storm from the opening never quite left.

item.title: Flock of the Tyrants (single)
item.description: An angry protest against automated license plate cameras and warrantless tracking that leans on the Fourth Amendment and the Carpenter decision. City halls and police who sign the contracts are cast as the villains, and the demand is to switch the cameras off.

item.title: Violent Light (single)
item.description: A furious track about distrust in vote counting, courts and judicial ethics, framed as darkness about to be flooded with light. Its central image is exposure, with the schemers dragged into a glare they cannot escape.

item.title: The Flock Betrayal (single)
item.description: A dense, wordy rap about local officials approving camera networks with no public vote. It paints each deal as a quiet betrayal and ends with a plea to set the open road free.

item.title: EVIL EYE CONTRACTS (single)
item.description: Another protest against license plate surveillance that tallies the cities and councils that signed on and the ones that pushed back. Each contract is framed as a betrayal of privacy, and the towns that said no are cheered on.

item.title: Carry the Star (single)
item.description: A gentle, encouraging song about the small inner light everyone carries and the way kindness passes it from hand to hand. It trades the catalog's usual thunder for warmth, legacy and quiet self-worth.

item.title: Anvil's Kiss (single)
item.description: An anthem of resilience for anyone who has been knocked down, comparing hardship to rough seas and a smith's anvil that toughen rather than break. Scars become medals, and the listener is told they have earned their own light.

item.title: Tinmouth Cathedral Volume 1 (album)
item.description: Tinmouth Cathedral Volume 1 builds a church out of scrap metal. Its titles cross sacred words with industrial ones, setting liturgy, vespers, an altar, a requiem and a sermon beside tin, rust, voltage, machines and distortion, from Rusted Industrial Liturgy and Grunge Machine Vespers to Shadow Pulse Requiem and EDM Rust Sermon, while Techno Tin Collapse and Cathedral Core Decay suggest the building is coming apart. Echoes run through the record too, from Tin Cathedral Reverberations and Echoes of Distortion to the closing Tinmouth Echo Chamber, as if the walls were answering back. The sound is pitched as a dueling beatbox battle, industrial techno squaring off against EDM grunge, with the two styles trading blows under the same rusted roof.

item.title: Blazing Stars (single)
item.description: Fathers, sons and ordinary men are forged like steel in this anthem of sacrifice, faith and liberty. The tree of liberty and a sky of burning stars carry the promise that simple people can turn the tide.

item.title: Sacred Steel (single)
item.description: A tribute to mothers and the women who pour themselves into their families, pushing back against the idea that nurturing is weakness. Lullabies, meals and sleepless nights become quiet victories with lasting power.

item.title: America 250 (single)
item.description: Written for the nation's 250th anniversary, it marches from Lexington and Valley Forge to the Delaware crossing and on to the present day. Embattled farmers, faith in God and the cost of freedom drive a proud, celebratory refrain.
